Perceptual Hausdorff Distance (PHD): A nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy that evaluates segmentation results by computing the Hausdorff distance between skeletonized cell membranes while incorporating a human-like tolerance threshold. The method is validated via a user study involving 20 subjects, demonstrating that PHD is significantly more aligned with human judgment than metrics like F1 score or IoU.
Strengths
✅ High-Impact Dataset Contribution
The U-RISC dataset is a substantial contribution. It is significantly higher in resolution and volume than prior benchmarks like ISBI2012 and SNEMI3D (e.g., Figure 1 on page 3 shows the image and pixel count comparisons).
The triple-iteration labeling and documentation of labeling stages (shown in Figure 3 on page 4) enhance reproducibility and provide rich ground truth references.
✅ Rigorous Subjective Validation
The user study (Sec. 3.2 and Figure 7 on page 13) adds empirical weight to the claim that current metrics do not align with human perception.
Results show that F1, IoU, and Dice align with human judgment only ~34% of the time, while PHD (with a tolerance value of 3) aligns at over 65% consistency (Figure 6 on page 8).
✅ Clear Metric Design
PHD is thoughtfully designed using skeletonization to isolate structural features and a tolerance distance to mimic perceptual flexibility (Figure 5 on page 6).
The mathematical formulation is well-grounded and interpretable.
✅ Experimental Breadth
The paper includes extensive comparisons across multiple classic segmentation models (U-Net, LinkNet, CASENet, etc.) and datasets (U-RISC, ISBI2012, SNEMI3D).
Table 1 (page 9) and Tables 5–6 (page 17) offer detailed multi-metric evaluations that highlight the gaps in classical metrics on U-RISC.
Weaknesses / Limitations
⚠️ Limited Generalization of PHD
While PHD aligns better with human perception in membrane segmentation, it is unclear how generalizable this metric is to other types of biomedical segmentation tasks (e.g., tumors, vessels). A broader application discussion would strengthen the impact.
⚠️ No Integration as a Loss Function
The authors mention potential future work in using PHD as a loss function for training models (Appendix VII), but do not explore it experimentally. Integrating evaluation metrics into training pipelines is increasingly standard and would strengthen the practical value.
⚠️ Dataset Availability
The paper notes that U-RISC will be released "upon acceptance" (Sec. 2.1), which may limit current reproducibility and impact assessment by other researchers.
⚠️ Moderate Novelty in Metric Design
While the PHD is insightful, its core design—skeletonization plus Hausdorff distance with tolerance—is conceptually straightforward. The innovation lies more in application context and validation than in technical complexity.
Suggestions for Improvement
Open Dataset Early: If feasible, provide early access to U-RISC for community benchmarking.
Explore PHD in Training: Conduct ablation studies or model training using PHD-based loss to assess benefits beyond evaluation.
Broader Metric Testing: Evaluate PHD on other structural segmentation tasks to argue for general applicability.
Optimize PHD Computation: Discuss runtime/performance trade-offs, especially when applied to large-scale or real-time pipelines.
Recommendation: Accept with Minor Revisions
This is a strong paper with meaningful contributions to dataset curation, evaluation methodology, and empirical analysis. The introduction of U-RISC and PHD is timely and well-executed. Some minor revisions—especially regarding generalizability and dataset release timing—would help elevate the impact further.

The proposed approach enhances the well-known GTD2 algorithm by incorporating second-order differences between successive value function estimates into the gradient update. The authors propose a new intrinsic reward mechanism, causal curiosity, which encourages agents to learn behaviors that produce outcome trajectories easily explainable by low-complexity models—thereby isolating individual causal factors. The approach is validated through extensive experimentation in simulated environments with varying physical properties such as mass, size, and shape. The learned behaviors and causal representations are shown to be semantically meaningful, sample-efficient, and transferable to downstream tasks with improved zero-shot generalizability.
Strengths
Innovative Conceptual Framework: The formulation of causal discovery as an active, curiosity-driven process is both intuitive and novel. The notion of using experimental behaviors as a tool for isolating causal factors aligns well with human scientific reasoning.
Clear Methodological Design: The authors clearly articulate their learning pipeline, involving an experiment planner, a causal inference module, and a hierarchical approach for discovering multiple causal factors sequentially.
Empirical Rigor:
Visualization of Learned Behaviors (Figure 2, page 7) convincingly demonstrates the interpretability and semantic value of the behaviors.

Hierarchical Representation Discovery: The recursive application of experimental clustering (Figure 4, page 8) builds a tree of binary causal embeddings, which is a clever and scalable design for disentangling multiple factors.
Reusability and Downstream Utility: Demonstrating how learned behaviors can bootstrap downstream tasks (lifting, pushing) adds practical value to the theoretical contributions.
Weaknesses
Scalability Limitations: The authors acknowledge (Appendix E, page 14) that their method—based on the one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) paradigm—scales poorly with the number of causal factors. This could limit its applicability in more complex, high-dimensional real-world environments.

Incorporate denser causal embeddings or continuous latent spaces and compare their performance and interpretability.
Include experiments with noise or confounding to test robustness under more realistic assumptions.
Introduce quantitative disentanglement metrics to benchmark representation quality against prior methods.
Evaluate scalability with more than 3-4 causal factors and analyze degradation in performance.

The RPI model significantly outperforms off-the-shelf LSTMs in long-term path integration tasks. It shows stronger correlation between internal states and absolute positions, enabling disambiguation in visually ambiguous environments—an essential feature of cognitive maps.

Limited Environmental Complexity
While the simplicity of the 2D environment is a design choice for interpretability, it restricts the model’s applicability to real-world tasks. Future work should test in richer, more dynamic 3D environments.

The retinal model, although inspired by biological systems, is still relatively abstract (e.g., Difference-of-Gaussians on landmarks). Incorporating raw pixel inputs could push this closer to practical deployment.

Summary
This paper proposes a novel methodology—PAC-BUS—for deriving generalization bounds in gradient-based meta-learning settings by combining two theoretical frameworks: uniform stability (for bounding base-level generalization) and PAC-Bayes theory (for meta-level generalization). The authors argue that the distinct challenges at each level of meta-learning warrant distinct analytical tools. The core contribution is Theorem 3, which provides a generalization bound with practical relevance, as it's both numerically computable and empirically tighter than competing approaches. The authors validate their theoretical claims through experiments on synthetic and real-world few-shot learning benchmarks, including the unit ball classification task, Mini-Wiki, and a challenging variant of Omniglot.
Strengths
Conceptual Innovation: The dual use of uniform stability and PAC-Bayes frameworks is elegant and well-justified, directly addressing the limitations of previous approaches that applied a single framework across both levels of meta-learning.
Theoretical Rigor: The generalization bounds are derived with care, clearly laid out, and connected to foundational works in learning theory (e.g., [29] for stability, [43] for PAC-Bayes).
Empirical Demonstration of Bound Tightness: Unlike many previous papers, this work explicitly computes and compares numerical values for generalization bounds, demonstrating that PAC-BUS provides significantly tighter bounds than alternatives like MR-MAML and MLAP-M.
Practical Regularization Scheme: The authors introduce a variant of their method (PAC-BUS(H)) that leverages the structure of their bound as a regularizer, yielding improved resistance to memorization in NME Omniglot tasks.
Broad Applicability: Though focused on few-shot learning, the paper suggests that the framework can be generalized to broader contexts, including reinforcement learning.
Weaknesses
Limited Empirical Superiority: While the PAC-BUS bounds are tighter, the test accuracy or loss does not significantly outperform other methods like MR-MAML or MAML in standard benchmarks. This limits the practical impact unless theoretical guarantees are prioritized.
Computational Intensity: The approach demands considerable computational resources, especially when evaluating PAC-Bayes regularizers across many posterior samples. The authors acknowledge that their results required weeks of AWS computation.
Scalability Issues: The bound becomes vacuous in high-dimensional settings such as large convolutional networks, due to the scaling of the KL-divergence term in PAC-Bayes. This limits its applicability to large-scale real-world problems.
Assumptions and Constraints: For the bounds to hold, assumptions like bounded loss and stability constraints are needed. These may be overly restrictive or require special architectures (e.g., networks with bounded Frobenius norms), which can hinder model flexibility.
No Convergence Guarantees: While the paper provides a theoretically grounded loss, it lacks a convergence analysis of the training algorithm, which is critical for practical deployment.
Suggestions for Improvement
Empirical Scaling: Explore approximations or surrogate metrics to reduce the computational overhead of PAC-Bayes term evaluation in high-dimensional models.

Specifically, the authors propose two forms of intrinsic motivation based on (1) information gain and (2) prediction error, allowing the agent to collect informative trajectories that facilitate task inference. This novel methodology enables efficient adaptation in both meta-training and test-time environments. Summary
This paper presents a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy called Prototype Recalls for addressing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning tasks. The proposed approach builds on metric learning by introducing a set of class-representative prototypes in a learned embedding space, where classification is performed based on proximity to these prototypes. To retain knowledge across tasks, the method uses prototype-based replay, matching newly embedded examples to previously stored class prototypes. Unlike prior approaches that rely on weight regularization or full data replay, this method only stores compact representations (prototypes and small example sets), making it memory-efficient. The authors validate the approach on standard benchmarks (Permuted MNIST, CIFAR10, miniImageNet) using both full-data and few-shot task protocols, showing superior average accuracy and retention performance across tasks.
Strengths
Clear Motivation and Novelty: The method directly addresses the inefficiency and scalability issues of existing rehearsal and regularization-based continual learning methods by leveraging prototype-based recall, which is conceptually elegant and computationally appealing.
Strong Empirical Performance:
The method consistently outperforms EWC, SI, MAS, iCARL, and FSR across multiple benchmarks and settings.
Particularly impressive results are shown in few-shot continual learning, where the method yields significant gains over alternatives (Figure 4 on page 8).
Efficient Memory Usage:
Memory scaling is explicitly managed through a dynamic allocation strategy (Section 2.3), balancing performance with limited capacity.
The comparison in Table 1 on page 9 underscores how the method achieves comparable or better performance with similar or lower memory budgets.
Interpretable and Intuitive Embedding Space:
The use of t-SNE visualizations (Figure 6, page 9) effectively demonstrates how class prototypes are organized and retained across tasks.
Algorithm Clarity:
The pseudocode (Algorithm 1, page 5) is concise and helpful, illustrating the training pipeline clearly.
Weaknesses
Limited Scope:
The method is designed specifically for classification tasks. The authors acknowledge in the conclusion that the approach doesn't yet generalize to regression or reinforcement learning problems, which limits its applicability.
Memory Growth with Tasks:
As discussed in Section 5, the number of stored prototypes grows linearly with the number of tasks, which could be problematic in long-horizon learning scenarios, despite being more compact than storing raw data or model parameters.
No Comparison with Generative Replay:
Although the paper justifies excluding generative methods due to architectural differences, this weakens the comparative analysis somewhat, especially given the popularity of generative replay approaches in continual learning.
Prototype Selection Strategy:
The paper uses random sampling to select examples for prototype computation (Section 2.2), which while simple, may not be optimal. A discussion or ablation of alternative selection methods (e.g., diversity-based or uncertainty-based sampling) would strengthen the work.
Suggestions for Improvement
Explore prototype compression or merging techniques to manage memory growth over many tasks.
Investigate application to non-classification tasks, such as reinforcement learning or regression.
Include additional baselines or variants using generative replay (even if only in supplementary material) for broader context.
Analyze the impact of different distance metrics or prototype update rules in the ablation study.

This paper proposes a well-justified and practical approach to a key problem in continual learning, with strong empirical evidence and sound theoretical motivation. Its efficiency, generalization to few-shot settings, and ease of implementation make it a valuable contribution to the field.

Summary
This paper addresses an underexplored but critical challenge in cross-modal matching—noisy correspondence, where pairs of multimodal data (e.g., image-text) are incorrectly aligned. The authors introduce the concept as a new paradigm of noisy labels, distinct from traditional label noise, by focusing on misaligned input pairs rather than incorrect class labels. To tackle this issue, they propose a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy called the Noisy Correspondence Rectifier (NCR). NCR leverages the memorization effect of deep neural networks to differentiate clean from noisy pairs and uses a co-teaching framework with adaptive soft-label rectification. A new triplet loss with a soft margin is also introduced to improve robustness. The method is validated on benchmark datasets (Flickr30K, MS-COCO, Conceptual Captions), outperforming existing methods under both synthetic and real noise conditions.
Strengths
Novel Problem Formulation:
The introduction of noisy correspondence fills a significant gap in cross-modal research. The distinction from label noise and partial alignment problems is clearly motivated and well-articulated.
Methodological Innovation:
The use of co-teaching with dual networks (A and B) and the application of GMM-based loss modeling to identify clean/noisy samples is well-grounded.
The adaptive prediction function (Eq. 5) is clever in removing the need for a hard similarity threshold.
The triplet loss with a soft margin (Eq. 6–7) effectively integrates rectified labels and enhances robustness against hard negatives.
Strong Experimental Results:
Across multiple datasets and under different noise levels (Table 1 & 2, pages 7–8), NCR consistently outperforms strong baselines like SCAN, SGRAF, and even SGR trained on clean data.
The method maintains competitive performance even in the absence of noise, showing no overfitting to the noisy-case scenario.
Comparisons to CLIP (Table 3, page 9) are insightful and reinforce the value of algorithmic solutions over brute-force scale.
Ablation and Analysis:
Thorough ablation studies (Table 4, page 10) confirm the contribution of each NCR component (co-divide, co-rectify, warmup). Visualization of GMM distributions and soft label predictions (Fig. 3) supports the method's interpretability.
Generalizability:
The method is shown to generalize to other matching architectures (e.g., NCR-SCAN), making it broadly applicable.
Weaknesses / Limitations
Dependency on Warmup:
The method requires an initial warmup phase with the original loss (Lw), which may still be influenced by noise. While mitigated by co-teaching, this phase might limit scalability or increase training complexity.
Soft Label Thresholding:
Although the adaptive prediction function removes the need for manual thresholds, it introduces heuristic choices (e.g., using the top 10% similarity margin as anchor), which might need tuning across datasets.
Limited Analysis on Failure Cases:
While noisy samples are visualized (Fig. 4, page 10), the paper lacks deeper analysis of borderline or ambiguous cases (e.g., semantically similar but technically misaligned pairs).
Real-world Generalization:
The Conceptual Captions dataset contains real noise, but a broader evaluation on other large-scale, real-world noisy datasets would strengthen the practical impact.
Suggestions for Improvement
Include additional real-world data scenarios where correspondence noise naturally occurs, such as social media or video-caption datasets.
Explore a lightweight variant of NCR that doesn't rely on full co-teaching, to reduce training cost.
Provide open benchmarks or tools to simulate noisy correspondence, encouraging further work in this new problem space.
Recommendation
Strong Accept
This paper opens up a new research direction in multimodal learning, backed by solid methodology and extensive evaluation. It makes a convincing case for handling noisy correspondences in cross-modal matching and provides practical, well-engineered solutions with promising results.

Summary
This paper introduces a novel methodology for parameter-efficient uncertainty quantification in deep learning, leveraging a mechanism called inducing weights. By augmenting standard neural network layers with small auxiliary weight matrices and using matrix normal distributions, the authors project uncertainty into a lower-dimensional latent space. This facilitates memory-efficient variational inference for Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) and deep ensembles.
A key technical contribution is the extension of Matheron’s rule for efficient posterior sampling under this setup, mitigating computational bottlenecks. The proposed method—when applied to architectures like ResNet-50—achieves competitive performance in terms of predictive accuracy, calibration (ECE), and robustness to distribution shifts, while reducing parameter count to ≤ 24.3% of a single deterministic model, even before pruning.
Strengths
Innovative Use of Inducing Weights: The idea of introducing low-dimensional inducing weights for each layer is both theoretically sound and practically impactful. It creates a bridge between sparse Gaussian Process (GP) approximations and deep learning models.
Efficient Sampling Strategy: Extending Matheron’s rule to matrix-variate distributions (Section 3.2, Fig. 1c) is a technically strong contribution that enables efficient sampling from the conditional posterior with significantly reduced computational cost.
Comprehensive Evaluation:
The method is benchmarked on toy regression, classification (CIFAR-10/100), and out-of-distribution detection.
Inducing-weight variants match or outperform fully factorized Gaussian (FFG) baselines in both accuracy and calibration (e.g., Table 2, page 7).
Strong parameter efficiency is demonstrated (Fig. 3, page 7), with >75% parameter savings.
Open-Source Tooling: The method is implemented in a PyTorch-compatible library (bayesianize), making it accessible to practitioners.
Pruning Compatibility: The approach can be combined with pruning strategies for further memory gains, unlike FFG-based methods that break the inference model post-hoc (Fig. 6, page 8).
Weaknesses
Limited Analysis of Scalability Beyond Vision Tasks:
While CIFAR and ResNet are popular benchmarks, applying this method to NLP (e.g., BERT) or reinforcement learning could further validate generality.
Some Complexity in Implementation:
Although the authors provide software support, the derivation and use of matrix normal distributions and extended Matheron’s rule may still deter users unfamiliar with Gaussian process theory.
Tuning Hyperparameters:
The need for careful selection of hyperparameters like λ_max and σ_max (as seen in Fig. 4, page 7) suggests that model calibration is sensitive to these choices.
Limited Societal Impact Discussion:
The paper does not explore potential misuse or risks associated with deploying uncertainty-aware systems in critical settings.

The paper is well-organized and clearly written. Diagrams like Fig. 1 (page 5) effectively illustrate the conceptual difference between traditional and inducing-weight-based sampling. Tables are informative and highlight the main trade-offs in computational and memory complexity (Table 1, page 6).
The mathematical derivations are dense but precise, and the authors provide ample appendices to clarify implementation and theoretical nuances.

Summary
This paper tackles the long-standing challenge of exploration in sparse-reward reinforcement learning (RL) environments. Instead of the traditional approach of combining intrinsic and extrinsic rewards into a single signal—which can lead to unstable training and suboptimal policies—the authors propose a hierarchical agent architecture called Scheduled Intrinsic Drive (SID). SID explicitly learns and schedules between two distinct policies: one for intrinsic motivation and one for extrinsic tasks. A nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy is introduced in the form of Successor Feature Control (SFC), a task-agnostic intrinsic reward based on changes in successor features, promoting exploration through bottleneck states.
The proposed approach is evaluated across diverse RL domains, including VizDoom, DeepMind Lab, and DeepMind Control Suite. Results show that SID with SFC not only improves exploration efficiency but also outperforms traditional reward-bonus techniques like ICM and RND in both sparse and distraction-heavy environments.
Strengths
Clear Motivation and Innovation:
The paper presents a well-reasoned critique of mixed-policy methods in intrinsic motivation and proposes a meaningful alternative with SID. The separation of exploration and exploitation through scheduling is conceptually elegant and practically effective.
Successor Feature Control (SFC):
The SFC reward is a strong conceptual and empirical contribution. It leverages a long-term representation of state transitions to identify bottlenecks, encouraging more structured exploration.
Strong Empirical Evaluation:
Experiments are thorough, spanning three environment classes with varying challenges (sparse rewards, visual complexity, distractor rewards). SID consistently outperforms baselines in these diverse tasks.
Ablation and Analysis:
The ablation studies convincingly show the advantages of SID over reward-bonus methods across all intrinsic reward types (ICM, RND, SFC). SID demonstrates robustness and stability.
Task Generality and Transferability:
Both SID and SFC are shown to be task-agnostic and easily integrable into standard off-policy frameworks like Ape-X DQN, promoting broader applicability.
Weaknesses
Scheduler Design:
Although the authors explore several scheduling strategies (random, switching, macro-Q, threshold-Q), none outperform the random scheduler consistently. This leaves open the question of how to optimally schedule between policies, which may limit performance in more complex domains.
Dependence on Off-Policy Learning:
The framework is dependent on off-policy methods like Ape-X DQN. Its compatibility with on-policy or model-based RL is not explored.

Develop and evaluate adaptive or learned scheduling mechanisms to further enhance SID.
Extend experiments to real-world or physically simulated robotic environments.
Explore compatibility with policy-gradient-based algorithms.
Investigate theoretical guarantees of SID, particularly in terms of convergence or sample complexity improvements.

The authors introduce a "residual feedback" estimator, which improves gradient estimation by using the difference between function values at consecutive time steps, rather than within the same time step as in traditional two-point methods. The work provides theoretical regret bounds under both convex and non-convex settings, supported by numerical experiments on non-stationary LQR control and resource allocation problems. The paper develops new regret bounds for both convex (Theorems 3.2, 3.4) and non-convex (Theorems 4.2, 4.3) online optimization problems.
It introduces assumptions (e.g., bounded variation) that are strictly weaker than those required in prior work such as Gasnikov et al. (2017), making the results more broadly applicable.

Here is a review of the paper “Persistent Homology Captures the Generalization of Neural Networks Without a Validation Set”:
Summary
This paper presents a novel methodology for monitoring the training and estimating the generalization capability of neural networks using tools from Algebraic Topology, specifically Persistent Homology (PH), without requiring a validation set. The authors construct weighted, directed graphs from neural network parameters at each training step, represent these as simplicial complexes, and track the evolution of persistence diagrams (PDs) over time. By computing distances between consecutive PDs (termed "homological convergence"), the paper shows a strong correlation between these distances and the validation accuracy across a variety of datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Reuters) and model configurations (MLPs and CNNs).
Strengths
Innovative Perspective: The application of Persistent Homology to track training dynamics without needing a validation set is a compelling and under-explored idea in deep learning. This approach tackles a fundamental issue in model evaluation and selection.
Methodological Rigor: The authors provide detailed theoretical background and a carefully constructed representation of neural networks using directed flag complexes, preserving topological structure without simplifying or approximating during computation.
Comprehensive Evaluation: The empirical study is robust, covering a range of datasets and hyperparameters. The strong correlation (Pearson > 0.8 in many cases) between PH distances and validation accuracy lends empirical credibility to the claims.
Control Experiments: The authors wisely include sanity checks such as varying input order to demonstrate that their topological distance metric is sensitive to learning dynamics rather than random noise.
Reproducibility: The code and outputs are reportedly provided, supporting transparency.
Weaknesses
Computational Scalability: A significant limitation is the high computational cost of the proposed method. It relies on exact PD distance calculations without simplifications, making it impractical for large-scale networks or real-time applications.
Lack of Predictive Modeling: While the correlation is shown convincingly, no model is proposed for predicting generalization error or early stopping criteria using the PH distances. This limits its immediate practical utility.
Restricted to MLPs: The methodology does not yet extend to convolutional layers or transformer-based models. CNNs are handled using frozen convolutional layers, limiting the relevance of the findings to real-world deep learning scenarios.
Missing Theoretical Justification for Correlation: While the correlation between PH distances and validation accuracy is empirically demonstrated, the paper lacks a deeper theoretical analysis explaining why this correlation holds.
Limited Interpretability: The meaning of topological features (e.g., birth/death of homological features) in terms of learning dynamics or function complexity remains abstract and unexplored.
Suggestions for Improvement
Develop approximate or scalable variants of the PH distance computation to broaden applicability.
Extend the method to convolutional and attention-based architectures.
Explore time-series modeling or predictive techniques based on homological convergence.
Provide more interpretability of topological features in terms of learning theory or neural network capacity.
Consider introducing visualizations or more intuitive explanations for readers unfamiliar with algebraic topology.
Overall Recommendation: Weak Accept / Borderline Accept
This paper introduces a creative and promising idea with strong empirical results and a rigorous methodology. However, its practical limitations and lack of broader applicability to modern architectures hold it back from a stronger recommendation. If the authors can address computational concerns and generalize the method beyond MLPs, the impact could be substantial.

Summary
This paper introduces a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy called Policy-extended Value Function Approximator (PeVFA), which augments the conventional value function in reinforcement learning (RL) by incorporating an explicit policy representation as input. This change enables the value function to generalize across different policies, rather than being tightly coupled to just one, as in traditional value function approximators (VFAs). The authors explore both global generalization (evaluating entirely new policies) and local generalization (generalizing to nearby policies along the policy improvement path). They provide theoretical guarantees for the generalization error bounds and demonstrate improved empirical performance of their PeVFA-based PPO (PPO-PeVFA) on multiple MuJoCo environments. In addition, the paper presents a framework for learning compact policy representations using either policy parameters or state-action pairs through end-to-end learning, auxiliary action prediction, and contrastive learning.
Strengths
Conceptual Novelty:
PeVFA introduces an important shift in how value functions are constructed, enabling generalization across policies, which is traditionally not feasible. This is a significant contribution to RL theory and practice.
Theoretical Rigor:
The authors provide strong theoretical foundations, including contraction bounds (Theorem 1 and Corollary 1) and a formal condition for improved approximation (Corollary 2), strengthening the claim that value generalization is not only possible but beneficial.
Empirical Validation:
PeVFA shows clear empirical improvements over traditional VFA-based PPO, especially in complex environments like Ant-v1 and Walker2d-v1 (Table 1, page 9). The comparison of approximation losses in Figure 3b and Figure 8 convincingly illustrates that PeVFA provides better starting points for learning.
Representation Learning Framework:
The authors propose two distinct methods for policy representation — Origin Policy Representation (OPR) from policy network parameters, and Surface Policy Representation (SPR) from trajectories — which are both shown to work effectively.
The inclusion of auxiliary objectives and contrastive learning significantly boosts representation quality (Table 1, page 9).
Clarity of Experiments:
The experiments are thorough, spanning 7 environments, with ablation on learning methods (E2E, CL, AUX), and t-SNE visualizations (Figure 5) to show representation quality.
Weaknesses
Scalability of Policy Representations:

This paper introduces a novel methodology for evaluating and understanding the performance of data augmentation in deep learning models by proposing two interpretable, model-sensitive metrics: Affinity and Diversity. Affinity measures how much augmented data resembles the original training distribution from the model’s perspective, while Diversity quantifies the effective increase in training data complexity due to augmentation. The paper conducts an extensive empirical study across 204 augmentations on CIFAR-10 and 225 on ImageNet, concluding that high test performance requires a balanced optimization of both Affinity and Diversity. It also explores augmentation as a regularization mechanism and analyzes the impact of switching augmentations off mid-training, revealing a "slingshot" effect that can enhance model performance and training efficiency
.
Strengths
Clarity and Motivation: The paper addresses a critical gap in the understanding of why and how data augmentations work, particularly moving beyond the simplistic assumption that "realistic" augmentations are best.
Novel Contributions:

Provides strong empirical support by evaluating hundreds of augmentation techniques across two major datasets.
Strong Empirical Rigor:
The analysis is extensive and well-structured, with robust statistical validation across multiple training runs (especially for CIFAR-10).
Experiments comparing static vs. dynamic augmentation clearly show that stochastic augmentations increase effective dataset size and boost performance.
Insightful Observations:
The concept that augmentations can act as regularizers, and that turning them off partway through training can improve performance (the “slingshot effect”), is both novel and practical.
Augmentations with high Diversity but low Affinity (e.g., Cutout, mixup) can still be highly effective, challenging prior assumptions
.
Relevance and Applicability: The findings are highly relevant for practitioners designing training pipelines, and the metrics could serve as tools in future AutoML or augmentation search systems.
Weaknesses
Computational Cost of Diversity: While Affinity is simple to compute, Diversity requires retraining models, making it less accessible for resource-constrained settings. The paper discusses proxy metrics but lacks extensive benchmarking of those proxies.
Limited Theoretical Underpinning: The paper is primarily empirical. While this is a strength for practical utility, it lacks a deeper theoretical framework that could explain why the metrics work so well beyond observed correlations.
ImageNet Results Are Less Robust: Unlike CIFAR-10, ImageNet experiments were only run once per configuration. This weakens the reliability of conclusions on a more complex dataset.

Include more lightweight or pre-training Diversity proxies to broaden the usability of the approach.
Explore theoretical connections between Affinity, Diversity, and generalization error bounds.
Run repeated ImageNet experiments for stronger statistical support.
Evaluate the framework on downstream tasks beyond image classification.

This paper makes a valuable contribution to the field of machine learning by advancing our understanding of the mechanisms behind data augmentation. The proposed Affinity and Diversity metrics offer a fresh, quantifiable perspective on a previously heuristic-driven domain. Despite some limitations in computational cost and theoretical depth, the insights are novel, actionable, and rigorously validated.

NFQI adapts traditional Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI) to learn group-specific policies while sharing information across groups via a structured Q-function: a shared component for both groups and a group-specific component for the "foreground" group.

Built upon unsupervised object segmentation methods like MONet and Slot Attention, LORL incorporates semantic supervision from natural language via a neuro-symbolic executor pipeline. The method aims to improve unsupervised segmentation and facilitate the grounding of object concepts without requiring explicit mask or property annotations. Experiments demonstrate that LORL outperforms baselines on datasets like Shop-VRB-Simple and PartNet-Chairs in segmentation accuracy, concept retrieval, visual reasoning, and referring expression comprehension.

Here is a detailed review of the paper titled "BeBold: Exploration Beyond the Boundary of Explored Regions":
Summary
This paper introduces BeBold, a novel methodology for intrinsic reward design in deep reinforcement learning (RL). BeBold proposes a criterion based on the regulated difference of inverse visitation counts to encourage agents to explore beyond the boundary of previously explored regions. Unlike traditional count-based or curiosity-driven intrinsic rewards, BeBold aims to address key challenges such as short-sightedness, detachment, and asymptotic inconsistency common in prior methods. The paper evaluates BeBold across a range of procedurally-generated environments (MiniGrid, NetHack, Montezuma’s Revenge), demonstrating significant gains over existing methods, particularly in hard-exploration scenarios.
Strengths
1. Conceptual Clarity and Motivation
The paper clearly identifies the pitfalls in existing intrinsic reward methods — especially the tendency of agents to get "trapped" in local optima due to misleading signals.
The proposed solution — using the difference in inverse visitation counts — is both simple and elegant. It directly targets boundary exploration while mitigating detachment.
2. Strong Empirical Results
BeBold solves all 12 challenging MiniGrid environments within 120M steps, outperforming baselines like RND, RIDE, ICM, and AMIGo, many of which fail on half of these tasks (Figures 2–3, Table 1).
On the NetHack Learning Environment, BeBold achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) across several tasks, such as "Staircase", "Pet", and "Scout" (Figure 7).
On Montezuma’s Revenge, BeBold achieves higher returns than RND for both CNN and RNN-based models, reaching 13,000 points with RNNs (Figure 8).
3. Rigorous Analysis
The authors conduct a thorough analysis of short-sightedness in count-based approaches using toy environments and real benchmarks (Tables 2–3, Figures 4–6).
Ablation studies confirm the importance of key design choices like episodic intrinsic reward restriction (ERIR) and reward clipping.
4. Simple, One-Stage Algorithm
Unlike approaches such as Go-Explore or AMIGo, BeBold does not require complex curriculum learning or teacher-student setups.
It generalizes well across tasks without task-specific tuning, as shown by consistent hyperparameters used across environments.
Weaknesses and Limitations
1. Noisy TV Problem
Like other curiosity-driven methods, BeBold is vulnerable to the Noisy TV issue, where agents are misled by stochastic transitions in the environment (e.g., random noise). This is explicitly acknowledged by the authors and affects performance on stochastic environments like Dynamic-Obstacles-5x5
.
2. Discrete State Assumption
BeBold relies on hashing for episodic visitation counts, which may not transfer well to continuous control tasks or environments without a clear state discretization. The paper suggests discretization as a workaround but does not provide experiments or solutions in continuous domains.
3. Limited Baseline Comparisons on Montezuma
Although BeBold shows promising results on Montezuma’s Revenge, the evaluation is preliminary. There’s no comprehensive comparison to other state-of-the-art algorithms beyond RND, and variance across multiple seeds is not reported.
Suggestions for Improvement
Address the Noisy TV problem, perhaps by integrating uncertainty estimation or filtering out stochastic sources.
Explore more scalable alternatives to episodic state hashing for continuous or high-dimensional environments.
Provide more comprehensive Montezuma experiments, including comparisons to Go-Explore and newer large-scale models (if feasible).
Include wall-clock training time comparisons to give practical insight into training efficiency.
Recommendation: Accept
The paper proposes a compelling and effective method that makes meaningful progress on exploration in sparse reward settings. Despite some limitations, the core idea is intuitive, the experiments are robust, and the contribution is significant. The nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy for intrinsic reward based on inverse visitation count difference is a valuable addition to the exploration toolkit in RL.

Summary
This paper introduces a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy called k-mixup, a generalization of the popular mixup regularization strategy for training deep neural networks. Unlike standard mixup, which interpolates between pairs of samples regardless of data structure, k-mixup interpolates between sets of k samples using optimal transport and displacement interpolation (under the Wasserstein metric). This approach aims to better preserve local structure in the data, particularly when it lies on a manifold or has cluster-based support.
The paper provides both theoretical justification and empirical results across various modalities (toy datasets, UCI datasets, images, and speech). Key claims include improved generalization, better label preservation, and enhanced adversarial robustness.
Strengths
Conceptual Innovation:
The generalization from mixup to k-mixup using optimal transport is elegant. It addresses known limitations of standard mixup (e.g., manifold intrusion) with minimal increase in complexity.
The use of displacement interpolation provides a principled way to respect the data manifold.
Theoretical Rigor:
The authors extend the regularization analysis of mixup to the k-mixup case, providing bounds and demonstrating how higher values of k lead to better label interpolation and cluster preservation (Section 2, Theorems 1 & 2).
The analysis is mathematically sound and covers both manifold support and label smoothness.
Empirical Coverage:
Results span toy, tabular, image, and speech datasets, consistently showing gains over standard mixup for k > 1 (e.g., Figure 3 and Figure 5).
Adversarial robustness (Figure 12) is significantly improved, with k-mixup outperforming 1-mixup under FGSM attacks.
Low Complexity Overhead:
The method is practical. Despite using optimal transport, the authors show that Hungarian matching has negligible overhead for typical k values (Section A).
Weaknesses
Marginal Gains in High Dimensions:
On high-dimensional datasets like CIFAR-10 or SVHN, gains over 1-mixup are statistically significant but small (often <1%). While this may be due to the limits of Euclidean geometry in high dimensions (as discussed), it somewhat dampens the practical impact of the method in these settings.
Limited Comparison to Baselines:
While the paper compares to manifold mixup and PuzzleMix conceptually, empirical comparisons to other mixup variants like AdaMix or AugMix are lacking.
Further experiments with adversarial training would provide more complete robustness evaluations.
Scalability Discussion:
While the authors show minimal overhead at k=32, they don't test k > 32 or address potential bottlenecks with large datasets or batch sizes. For example, would the method remain efficient on ImageNet-scale datasets?
Suggestions for Improvement
Include results on more modern datasets (e.g., TinyImageNet, ImageNet-100) and more robust baselines (e.g., CutMix, AugMix).
Evaluate on additional downstream tasks like semi-supervised learning or domain adaptation, where manifold-aware mixup could shine.
Explore adaptive selection of k based on local data density or confidence metrics.
Recommendation
Accept with minor revisions
The paper presents a thoughtful and well-supported extension of mixup, with clear theoretical insights and broad empirical validation. While improvements are dataset-dependent and more baseline comparisons could strengthen the case, the simplicity and effectiveness of the method make it a valuable contribution to data augmentation strategies in deep learning.

Paper Review
Summary
This paper introduces a novel methodology for improving adversarial robustness in deep neural networks (DNNs) by allowing non-uniform perturbations during adversarial training (AT). The key innovation lies in adapting perturbation bounds to reflect empirical data distributions, feature correlations, and domain knowledge rather than relying on uniform norm constraints typically used in computer vision. The authors propose two main techniques: a Mahalanobis distance-based constraint and weighted norms derived from Pearson correlation, Shapley values, or manual masking of immutable features. Experimental results across three real-world tasks (malware detection, credit risk prediction, and spam detection) demonstrate that models trained with non-uniform perturbations significantly outperform standard approaches in both defense success rate and robustness certification.
Strengths
Strong Motivation and Novelty: The authors convincingly argue that uniform norm-bounded perturbations are unrealistic for non-vision domains such as cybersecurity and finance. Their method enables adversarial training to respect semantic feature constraints.
Technical Rigor: The theoretical foundation includes a detailed treatment of Mahalanobis distance-based constraints, γ-consistency analysis (Theorem 2.1), and certified robustness via both LP (Theorem 4.1) and randomized smoothing (Theorem 4.2).
Comprehensive Experiments: The authors test their approach across three diverse domains with realistic, domain-specific attack models. In all cases, non-uniform perturbations improved robustness without significantly sacrificing clean accuracy.
Robust Certification: Modifications to LP and randomized smoothing methods for non-uniform perturbation bounds show improved certification margins and success rates compared to uniform approaches (e.g., Table 3 and 4 on pages 9 and 10).
Practical Relevance: The methods do not require test-time access to raw data or adversary knowledge, making them generalizable and more feasible in real-world deployments.
Weaknesses
Assumption of Gaussian Distributions: The γ-consistency metric and robustness proofs assume Gaussian-distributed data, which may not hold in practice for all tabular or binary feature sets (e.g., malware datasets).
Limited Analysis on Clean Accuracy Tradeoffs: While defense success rates are extensively reported, the impact on clean accuracy—especially for stronger attacks—is not always emphasized (although present in appendix tables).
Dependency on Feature Attribution Methods: Approaches like SHAP or Pearson correlation may introduce noise or bias if the attributions are misaligned with true model behavior.
No Formal Comparison with Other Non-uniform Works: While the authors discuss related work [25], they could provide clearer empirical or conceptual comparisons with alternative non-uniform certification methods.

The paper is well-organized and clearly written.
Visualizations (e.g., Figure 1 on page 5 and Figure 2 on page 8) effectively illustrate the superiority of non-uniform approaches in both visual embedding and defense success rate.
Appendices are appropriately used to offload technical details.

This paper presents a novel methodology for evaluating the disentanglement of deep generative models using topological properties of the learned data manifold. The authors propose an unsupervised and a supervised metric based on persistent homology and Wasserstein Relative Living Times (W. RLTs) to assess the topological similarity among conditional submanifolds generated by varying latent dimensions. Their approach removes the need for auxiliary classifiers, dataset-specific preprocessing, or prior knowledge of the data structure, offering a model-agnostic, geometry-driven alternative for disentanglement evaluation.
Strengths
Theoretical Innovation:
The use of topological invariants (especially homology) to measure disentanglement is conceptually fresh and rigorous.

.
Methodological Clarity:
Clear algorithmic descriptions (e.g., Algorithm 1 on page 5) help demystify the process for generating and comparing W. RLTs.

Practical Usefulness:
The unsupervised metric is entirely model- and dataset-agnostic.
The supervised variant is label-efficient, avoiding reliance on additional encoders or classifiers that can introduce bias
.

Extensive experiments across 10 generative models and 3 datasets (dSprites, CelebA, CelebA-HQ) show that the proposed metrics (μ and μ_SUP) align well with existing methods such as MIG and classifier-based scores

Opens New Directions:
Highlights limitations of symmetry and suggests extensions, like measuring other topological invariants beyond homology (Figure 6, page 7), hinting at fertile ground for future research.

Computational Complexity:
Persistent homology computations, especially with Wasserstein barycenters, are computationally expensive, potentially limiting scalability to high-dimensional datasets or models with many latent variables.
Limited Applicability in Symmetric or Trivial Manifolds:
The method assumes asymmetry in the data manifold to detect disentanglement, which may not hold in synthetic datasets with symmetric factors (noted as a limitation in Section 3.2 and Figure 6).

Improve interpretability: Provide empirical thresholds or guidelines for interpreting μ scores more intuitively.
Explore robustness to embedding choice: Investigate how sensitive the results are to the specific embedding used for RLT calculation.

This paper makes a strong and meaningful contribution to disentanglement research by introducing a geometrically grounded and model-agnostic evaluation framework. This paper presents a novel approach to uncertainty quantification in image classification using a conformal prediction-based method called Regularized Adaptive Prediction Sets (RAPS). The authors build upon prior work in conformal prediction, particularly Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS), and introduce a regularization mechanism that significantly reduces the size of prediction sets without compromising their statistical coverage guarantees. The resulting RAPS method retains the simplicity and computational efficiency of Platt scaling while offering finite-sample coverage guarantees for any classifier and dataset.
By tempering noisy tail probabilities through a regularization term, RAPS produces smaller and more stable prediction sets. The method is validated on challenging benchmarks like ImageNet and ImageNet-V2 across a suite of standard classifiers (e.g., ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, etc.), showing superior performance over naive, APS, and LAC (Least Ambiguous Classifier) baselines. The paper emphasizes the adaptiveness of RAPS—its ability to yield smaller prediction sets on easier examples and larger ones on harder cases. This property is shown to be crucial in real-world applications like medical diagnostics.
The authors describe their Unоvеl mеthоdоlоgy with clear mathematical grounding and offer extensive empirical evaluation, including considerations for hyperparameter selection and adaptiveness metrics.
Strengths
Sound Theoretical Foundation:
The method is grounded in conformal prediction theory, offering distribution-free, finite-sample coverage guarantees, a notable improvement over softmax-based probability estimates or heuristic calibration.
Improved Prediction Set Size:
RAPS consistently reduces the average size of prediction sets compared to APS, often by a factor of 5–10 (e.g., from 19 to 2 classes for ResNeXt-101 at 90% confidence on ImageNet)
.
Adaptiveness and Practical Relevance:
The adaptiveness of RAPS—smaller sets for easy cases and larger ones for harder examples—makes it highly practical, especially for high-stakes applications like medicine.
Extensive Empirical Validation:
The paper offers comprehensive benchmarks on 9 classifiers and across two large datasets (ImageNet and ImageNet-V2) under different α levels (10% and 5%)
.
The figures and tables (e.g., Figure 2, Tables 1–4) effectively demonstrate the empirical benefits in both coverage and set size.
Code Availability and Reproducibility:
The authors provide a PyTorch-compatible codebase, promoting reproducibility and real-world application.

Randomization in Predictions:

Although tuning procedures are included in Appendix E, a more intuitive interpretation or guidance on these hyperparameters in the main text would benefit practitioners.

Paper Review
Summary
This paper presents a novel methodology for improving Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by proposing a piece-wise polynomial filtering model, dubbed PP-GNN. It addresses the challenge of performance degradation in GNNs when applied to heterophilic graphs, where connected nodes often have dissimilar labels—a known weakness of standard GNN architectures.
The core innovation is the use of multiple adaptive polynomial filters, each operating on distinct subintervals of the graph's eigenspectrum. This design enables the model to learn complex, task-specific frequency responses that better align with the structural properties of diverse graph types. The method generalizes and improves upon GPR-GNN by adding flexibility in modeling high- and low-frequency components separately, which is shown to be more effective in a wide range of settings.
The model is theoretically grounded with proofs showing that the filter space it learns is strictly larger than that of existing polynomial filter methods. Empirically, PP-GNN shows strong and consistent improvements—up to 10%—over baselines across both heterophilic and homophilic benchmarks.
Strengths
Innovative Filtering Design:
The move from a single global polynomial to a sum of localized polynomial filters is elegant and theoretically justified. The piece-wise modeling captures complex frequency characteristics that traditional models miss.
Robust Empirical Validation:
Extensive experiments (Tables 1 & 2, pp. 7–8) on 15 datasets (heterophilic and homophilic) show consistent gains. Particularly strong improvements are reported on challenging heterophilic datasets like Squirrel and Chameleon.
Strong Theoretical Contributions:
The authors prove that the expressiveness of the filter class in PP-GNN is strictly greater than that of GPR-GNN and that the extended filter space leads to better approximations of latent optimal filters (Theorem 4.1 & 4.2, p. 6–7).
Scalability Considerations:
The authors smartly leverage top and bottom-k eigencomponents and amortize eigendecomposition costs, making the method practical for large graphs (as seen in the experiments on Flickr and OGBN-Arxiv, Table 2, p. 7).
Ablation and Interpretability:
The frequency response plots (Figure 2, p. 8) and filter decomposition studies (Table 3, p. 9) offer clear evidence of how different components contribute to the final performance—adding credibility to the design.
Weaknesses
Dependence on Eigen-decomposition:
While mitigated with top/bottom eigenpair approximations, the need for eigendecomposition still adds overhead and may not scale well to million-node graphs without further optimization or approximations.
Limited Discussion on Graph Dynamics:
The method assumes a static graph structure. Applications involving dynamic or streaming graphs (e.g., temporal graphs) are not discussed.
Overhead vs. Gain Tradeoff:
Although the performance gains are significant, the training times (Table 12, p. 26) are roughly 2× GPR-GNN and 4× GCN. While acceptable in research, this could be a bottleneck in latency-sensitive real-world applications.
Minor Comments
The choice of polynomial degree and number of partitions (filters) could be sensitive to the dataset. More guidelines or heuristics on this would benefit practitioners.
The authors acknowledge the privacy implications of their model (Section 8, p. 10), which is an important and often overlooked consideration.
Recommendation
Accept (Strong Accept)

Through carefully designed experiments using referential games with partial observations, the paper identifies how message similarity (language agreement) and communication success rate are influenced by group size and connectivity.

Summary
This paper investigates the tightness of PAC-Bayes generalization bounds in the small data regime (e.g., 30–60 datapoints), a setting where traditional test set bounds suffer due to the need to withhold data from training. The authors aim to determine how tight PAC-Bayes bounds can be in theory and practice, using Germain et al.'s generic PAC-Bayes theorem as a unifying framework. They show theoretically that the tightest possible bound under this framework coincides with a known Catoni bound when customized to each dataset, and derive a lower bound on the tightest achievable bound in expectation across datasets. The authors also provide empirical results using meta-learning to jointly optimize learning algorithms, priors, and bound forms. The results show that, in some settings, PAC-Bayes bounds can be competitive with or even outperform Chernoff test set bounds, though not the binomial tail bounds.
A key contribution is the introduction of a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy for learning convex functions Δ that optimize the PAC-Bayes bound, using neural networks.
Strengths
Theoretical Depth and Clarity:
The authors provide strong theoretical analysis (e.g., Theorem 4, Corollary 3) that tightly characterizes the limits of the generic PAC-Bayes framework.
Figure 1 gives a helpful visual map showing the relationship between PAC-Bayes bounds and test set bounds, clarifying where improvements may be possible and where they are fundamentally limited.
Methodological Innovation:
A standout contribution is the meta-learning of convex Δ functions using constrained neural networks, pushing the practical application of PAC-Bayes theory forward.
Empirical Validation:
Carefully designed experiments (e.g., Figures 2–4) on synthetic 1D classification tasks convincingly demonstrate that PAC-Bayes can be nearly optimal in certain settings when bounds are tailored through meta-learning.
The authors meta-learn not only the posterior and learning algorithms but also data-dependent priors (DDPs), providing a comprehensive study.
Relevance and Novelty:
The paper addresses a timely and under-explored question: how to get tight generalization bounds when data is scarce—a situation common in real-world applications such as healthcare.
Weaknesses and Limitations
Limited Practical Scope:
The experiments are confined to synthetic 1D binary classification tasks. While this makes meta-optimization tractable, it leaves open questions about scalability and effectiveness on real-world, high-dimensional datasets.
No Formal Validation of Conjectured Bound:
While Corollary 3 introduces the conjectured PAC-Bayes-kl bound, the paper stops short of proving its validity. Open Problem 1 acknowledges this gap.
Assumptions on Data:
The paper assumes i.i.d. data and bounded losses, which may not hold in many small-data applications (e.g., temporally correlated or noisy medical datasets). This restricts generalizability.
Experimental Comparisons:
Although the binomial tail test set bound outperforms PAC-Bayes bounds in terms of tightness, the authors could further discuss why this bound cannot be achieved within the PAC-Bayes framework (only briefly mentioned in Corollary 3 and Figure 1).
Impact and Contributions
This work makes substantial contributions to understanding PAC-Bayes bounds:
It provides tight characterizations of theoretical limits within an established generic PAC-Bayes framework.
It develops a meta-learning pipeline that optimizes not only posteriors but also prior selection and the form of the bound itself.
It raises and clearly articulates important open problems (e.g., whether PAC-Bayes bounds can match binomial tail bounds, or whether the conjectured PAC-Bayes-kl bound is always attainable).
These contributions are likely to influence both theoretical and applied work in generalization bounds and meta-learning.
Recommendations
For Practitioners: This paper offers a useful framework for improving generalization bounds in small data tasks, especially in synthetic or well-controlled environments. However, practical deployment will require additional validation in higher-dimensional and non-i.i.d. settings.
For Researchers: The paper opens up meaningful theoretical questions (especially Open Problems 1 and 2) that are ripe for further exploration.
Overall Evaluation:

Conceptual Simplicity vs. Complexity Trade-off: While the idea of taking notes is intuitive, maintaining a note dictionary and calculating contextual averages introduces a layer of complexity. For very large corpora or vocabularies, note storage could still pose scalability concerns despite the authors' filtering strategy (100–500 frequency words).
Limited Scope of Evaluation: The experiments focus primarily on GLUE tasks. It would be beneficial to evaluate TNF on other settings such as question answering, summarization, or multilingual corpora to understand its generalizability.
Lack of Direct Comparison to Other Memory-Augmented Approaches: Although the authors distinguish TNF from traditional memory-augmented models, a head-to-head empirical comparison with such methods (e.g., REALM or KNN-LM) would strengthen the contribution claim.

Explore compression or sparsification techniques for storing the note dictionary to enhance scalability.
Include human-readable examples (e.g., before/after predictions) to illustrate qualitative benefits of TNF in rare word contexts.
Compare with retrieval-augmented models or contextual sub-word embeddings directly in future work.
Conclusion
"Taking Notes on the Fly" introduces a clever and effective mechanism for improving language pre-training by better handling rare words. Its impact lies in making large-scale pre-training more efficient without sacrificing accuracy or increasing deployment cost. The paper is well-structured, empirically robust, and practically relevant, making it a strong contribution to the field of efficient NLP pre-training.

Review of “NBDT: Neural-Backed Decision Tree”
Summary
The paper presents a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy called Neural-Backed Decision Trees (NBDTs) aimed at improving both accuracy and interpretability of deep neural networks, especially for image classification tasks. NBDTs work by replacing the final linear classification layer of a neural network with a soft decision tree that uses path probabilities for inference. Unlike traditional decision trees, NBDTs are trained using a surrogate "tree supervision loss" and use induced hierarchies built from model weights rather than predefined or data-driven taxonomies. The approach demonstrates state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet, while providing meaningful interpretability benefits.
Strengths
Joint Optimization of Accuracy and Interpretability:
The paper addresses a longstanding challenge—trading off model accuracy for interpretability—by proposing a model that performs competitively while maintaining interpretable properties like sequential decisions, pure leaves, and non-ensembled predictions
.
Innovative Use of Weight-Induced Hierarchies:
Instead of relying on traditional hierarchies (like WordNet or information gain), the authors build hierarchies directly from pretrained model weights, showing superior performance across datasets (see Table 2 on page 6). This approach prevents overfitting and respects visual similarity over conceptual similarity.
Soft Decision Tree Inference:
The authors employ “soft” path probabilities to tolerate uncertain decisions and recover from early mistakes in the hierarchy (illustrated well in Figure 1C on page 3). This is a significant improvement over “hard” decision tree paths, which are brittle and unforgiving.
Comprehensive Evaluation:
The model is rigorously tested across datasets and architectures. It also includes ablation studies (Table 3), hierarchy comparisons (Table 2), and interpretability surveys with human participants (Section 5), which support the claimed benefits.
Interpretability Evaluation with Human Subjects:
Multiple surveys demonstrate that users are more capable of identifying incorrect classifications using NBDT explanations (Section 5.1) and trust NBDT more than saliency maps (Section 5.3). The method even helps diagnose faulty dataset labels using path entropy (Section 5.4, Figure 6 on page 9).
Minimal Architectural Overhead:
NBDTs can be applied to any pretrained classifier without requiring significant architectural changes, making the approach modular and easy to integrate into existing systems.
Weaknesses
Dependency on Pretrained Models:
While NBDT’s induced hierarchies from pretrained weights are effective, the paper notes performance drops when using hierarchies from partially trained models (Table 4). This reliance may limit applicability in scenarios where full pretraining is not feasible.
Scalability to Ultra-Large Hierarchies:
The method is tested up to ImageNet scale, but the construction and maintenance of the induced hierarchies and soft decision inference could pose challenges at even larger class scales (e.g., 10,000+ classes), though this is not explicitly discussed.
Lack of Clarity on Real-Time Deployment Costs:
While inference paths are efficient, the soft tree structure introduces probabilistic computation at each node. The paper does not quantify the computational cost at inference time compared to a standard softmax layer, which may matter for real-time or edge deployments.
Limited Semantics in Intermediate Labels:
Though WordNet is used to label internal decision nodes (Section 3.3), the authors themselves acknowledge that WordNet lacks concepts tied to abstract or visual similarity (e.g., “aquatic” or “cylindrical”). This limits the semantic clarity of the decision path for certain classes.
Impact and Contributions
This paper makes a valuable contribution to the field of explainable AI by providing a compelling hybrid between decision trees and deep neural networks. It challenges the prevailing notion that interpretability and accuracy are mutually exclusive. Its applicability to real-world domains such as medical imaging or autonomous driving—where understanding model decisions is essential—is particularly noteworthy.
Overall Recommendation
Strong Accept.
This paper introduces a novel and practical approach to interpretable deep learning that demonstrates compelling performance and real human usability in evaluation. The clarity of the methodology, strength of experimental results, and real-world applicability justify its place in top-tier venues focused on AI, ML, or computer vision.

Summary
This paper proposes a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy for representing partially written programs in the context of inductive program synthesis. The key innovation is blended abstract semantics, which merges concrete execution with learned neural representations to more accurately and flexibly reason about incomplete code. Drawing on ideas from abstract interpretation, the authors use neural module networks to build compositional, interpretable encodings of partial program states, enabling execution-guided synthesis even when concrete semantics are unavailable (e.g., due to holes or incomplete expressions).
Blended semantics helps determine whether a partial program is on the right track toward satisfying a specification and allows the system to better navigate the combinatorial space of possible programs. The approach is evaluated across three domains—tower building (with loops), list processing (with higher-order functions), and string editing—showing consistent improvements over neural-only or syntax-based baselines.
Strengths
Conceptual Innovation:
The paper introduces a unique hybrid neuro-symbolic approach, grounded in classic static analysis theory (abstract interpretation), but enhanced with modern representation learning.
Generality and Flexibility:
Blended semantics elegantly handle cases where parts of a program can be concretely executed while others remain abstract. This is particularly useful in languages with complex features like loops or higher-order functions.
Empirical Validation:
In the tower-building domain (Figure 4, page 7), the blended model outperforms neural-only and RNN baselines.
In list processing (Figure 6, page 8), it demonstrates clear advantages over DeepCoder and neural-only methods, especially with complex lambdas.
In string editing (Figure 7, page 8), the blended model performs well even without requiring DSL modification, unlike REPL-based systems.
Theoretical Grounding:
The blend of neural abstract semantics with concrete execution is not only empirically strong but rooted in a meaningful reinterpretation of abstract interpretation.
Modularity:
Neural modules per function (e.g., for +, map, etc.) ensure extensibility and facilitate learning from compositional program structure.
Weaknesses
Limitations in Loop Handling:
As acknowledged in Appendix C (page 15), loops are treated uniformly as higher-order functions without fixpoint analysis. This could potentially limit expressiveness or precision in more sophisticated settings.
Lambda Representations:
The handling of lambda expressions is simplified—arguments are embedded without actual evaluation during representation (Appendix A, page 12). This could limit generalization when lambda behavior becomes more complex.
Search Cost:
While blended semantics improve success rates, they may incur additional computation due to dynamic switching between neural and concrete evaluations. This tradeoff is not thoroughly quantified.
Dependence on Training Data:
The model’s ability to generalize seems tied to a well-covered training set (e.g., 480k–2M samples per domain). The performance under more data-scarce regimes is unexplored.
Suggestions for Improvement
Introduce more rigorous semantics for loops, perhaps via a learned fixpoint model.
Explore advanced lambda representations, possibly integrating symbolic evaluation during training.
Conduct ablation on neural module capacity or architecture to better understand representational limits.
Evaluate performance in few-shot or data-limited settings to assess generalization robustness.
Overall Evaluation
This paper makes a strong contribution to the field of program synthesis by introducing a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy that meaningfully combines symbolic and neural reasoning. The idea of blended abstract semantics stands out as a practical and theoretically motivated bridge between learned representations and program behavior prediction. The results show clear advantages across a range of synthesis tasks, and the modular design allows for further exploration and enhancement.

Here is a review of the paper titled "Proper Measure for Adversarial Robustness":
Summary
This paper critiques the widely-used standard adversarial accuracy metric for evaluating classifier robustness, arguing that it fails to capture true robustness, especially in scenarios where invariance-based adversarial examples exist. The authors propose a novel methodology called genuine adversarial accuracy, which aims to address shortcomings in the standard definition by avoiding overlapping perturbation regions and ignoring adversarial examples that change the perceptual class.
The paper further proves that a 1-nearest neighbor (1-NN) classifier maximizes genuine adversarial accuracy under certain assumptions (e.g., exclusive class membership), and uses this to explain potential trade-offs between clean test accuracy and robustness. The authors empirically evaluate their approach using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets and link adversarial training outcomes with the behavior of 1-NN classifiers.
Strengths
Clear Identification of a Problem: The authors convincingly demonstrate that standard adversarial accuracy may favor overly invariant models and fail to distinguish between perceptually valid and invalid perturbations.
Innovative Metric: The definition of genuine adversarial accuracy is mathematically rigorous and conceptually appealing. By excluding overlapping regions and using Voronoi boundaries, the metric better aligns with intuitive notions of robustness.
Theoretical Contributions: Theorems proving that 1-NN classifiers maximize this new metric provide strong theoretical grounding and insight into the behavior of robust models.
Empirical Validation: The analysis on MNIST and CIFAR-10 shows that adversarially trained models partially mimic 1-NN behavior, especially on CIFAR-10, adding practical relevance to the theoretical claims.
Insightful Discussion on Distance Metrics: The discussion linking robustness, generalization, and the choice of distance metric provides a compelling explanation for the accuracy-robustness tradeoff observed in practice.
Weaknesses
Assumption of Exclusive Class Membership: The analysis heavily relies on this assumption, which may not hold in many real-world scenarios. This limits the general applicability of the conclusions.
Computational Complexity: Calculating genuine adversarial accuracy, especially by exact perturbation norms, could be computationally expensive. The authors acknowledge this but do not offer scalable alternatives beyond theoretical suggestions.
Limited Empirical Diversity: The experiments are limited to MNIST and CIFAR-10, which may not generalize to more complex datasets or tasks (e.g., NLP or object detection).
Over-Reliance on 1-NN Analogy: While the connection to 1-NN classifiers is novel and interesting, it may oversimplify the complexity of deep model behaviors, especially in high-dimensional and feature-engineered spaces.
Suggestions for Improvement
Extend experiments to more challenging datasets (e.g., ImageNet) to evaluate the generalizability of the proposed metric.
Investigate the computational feasibility of approximating genuine adversarial accuracy in large-scale settings.
Explore how the methodology applies when the exclusive class assumption is violated, potentially with soft-label or probabilistic labeling schemes.
Consider evaluating how the genuine adversarial accuracy metric correlates with human perception of robustness in real-world adversarial scenarios.
Recommendation
Accept with Minor Revisions
This paper makes a significant conceptual and theoretical contribution to the field of adversarial robustness. The introduction of genuine adversarial accuracy addresses a longstanding limitation in robustness evaluation, and the linkage to 1-NN classifiers opens new avenues for understanding the robustness-generalization tradeoff. While some practical aspects need further exploration, the work is a valuable addition to the literature.

Here is a detailed review of the paper "Out-of-Distribution Prediction with Invariant Risk Minimization: The Limitation and an Effective Fix":
Summary
This paper investigates the limitations of Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) in the context of out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction under conditions of strong spurious correlations—specifically, what the authors term "strong Λ spuriousness". The core insight is that IRM, while designed to learn invariant causal features across training domains, can inadvertently learn spurious representations (e.g., the domain label itself) if such representations satisfy the IRM constraint.
To illustrate this failure mode, the authors introduce a new benchmark, Colored MNIST Plus (CMNIST+), which extends the standard Colored MNIST by adding a third test domain and enforcing stronger dependencies between spurious features, the domain, and the label. They then propose a nоvеl mеthоdоlоgy that combines IRM with Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM) using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and adversarial training (IRM-MMD and IRM-ACDM). Experimental results demonstrate that these combined methods outperform standard IRM, especially under strong Λ spuriousness.
Strengths
Clear Problem Formulation:
The paper clearly articulates the failure scenario of IRM under strong spurious correlations. The causal diagram in Figure 1 (page 1) and the subsequent theoretical analysis effectively support this argument.
Dataset Contribution:
The creation of the CMNIST+ dataset is a valuable contribution. It is specifically designed to expose the weaknesses of IRM by simulating stronger and more complex spurious correlations than the original CMNIST. This makes it a useful tool for benchmarking future OOD algorithms.
Empirical Evidence:
The performance drop of IRM under strong Λ spuriousness is well-demonstrated in Figure 2 (page 3), while Figure 4 (page 5) further confirms how the issue emerges as the dataset gradually transitions from CMNIST to CMNIST+. This progression is well-designed and compelling.
Effective Fix:
The proposed methods (IRM-MMD and IRM-ACDM) are not only simple and theoretically grounded, but also empirically validated. As shown in Table 3 (page 8), they outperform IRM and other baselines like ERM, MMD, and EIIL in test accuracy under high spuriousness settings.
Theoretical Backing:
The analysis sections (Appendix B) provide theoretical justification for why IRM can fail and why CDM helps, including detailed derivations of expected accuracies for various feature learning strategies.
Weaknesses
Evaluation Scope:
The experiments are only conducted on a single semi-synthetic dataset (CMNIST+). While CMNIST+ is well-motivated, broader evaluations on natural datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, or WILDS) would help validate the generality of the proposed fix.
Lack of Real-world Tasks:
The work focuses on a synthetic setting, and while it effectively isolates the problem, there’s no demonstration on more realistic or industry-relevant tasks where spurious correlations are common.
Limited Analysis of Trade-offs:
While IRM-ACDM and IRM-MMD show better performance, the added complexity (especially adversarial training) and the computational cost are not discussed. A deeper analysis of trade-offs between performance and efficiency would improve the practical appeal of the method.
CDM Alone is Ineffective:
As admitted by the authors themselves, CDM alone is not sufficient. While this is clearly presented (page 7), it might suggest that the proposed fix is highly dependent on IRM and not broadly applicable on its own.
Recommendation
Accept with minor revisions.
This paper makes a significant theoretical and empirical contribution to understanding and mitigating the limitations of IRM in OOD prediction. The identification of strong Λ spuriousness as a failure case is important and novel. The proposed fix—combining IRM with CDM—is well-motivated and empirically strong. However, for broader impact and generalization, the paper would benefit from evaluations on additional real-world datasets and a discussion of computational trade-offs.
Suggested Revisions
Include results on at least one real-world dataset (e.g., WILDS) to demonstrate generalizability.
Discuss the computational overhead of IRM-ACDM and IRM-MMD versus IRM and ERM.
Add qualitative analysis (e.g., visualization of learned features) to support claims on causal versus spurious feature learning.
